items.text: For a field label or column header, use type.label. Don't use type.caption. Caption is too faint for a label people must read.
For keyboard focus, use button/focus-ring at border-width.focus. Don't use removing the outline. Keyboard users must always see where they are.
For the gap around a focus ring, use border-width.focus-offset. Don't use a ring that touches the control. The ring stands clear of the control, so readers see focus on any fill.

items.text: For a text in a table cell, use type.data. Don't use a mono font. It equals body here. Tables are rare and read row by row. Cells use the reading face, so a row reads like a sentence.
For a something that grows past one line, use radius.element. Don't use radius.surface. Text areas and list items share the control corner, so a form reads as one family.
For a button inside a field, use size.control.compact. Don't use size.control.default. A clear or show button must fit inside the field around it.

content-q2.why: One idea per screen keeps reading calm.

why: radius.8: We use an 8px corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a warm tone, by brand convention. A rounded radius does this by curving the edge enough to feel soft, while the sides stay straight. So controls feel friendly next to long text and never compete with it, because the brand is warm (brand.q1), corners are rounded (shape.values) and each screen holds one idea (content.q2).

radius.8: We use the 8px control corner for boxes that grow in order to keep their role, as objects of one family, by inheritance from the control corner. The same radius does this by giving a list item or a text area the curve of the controls beside it. So fields and rows read as one family, because the control corner is rounded, not a pill (shape.values), and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

items.text: For a number in a table, use type.body. Don't use a mono font. Tables are rare and read row by row, so digits never need to line up in columns. A mono font would break the reading voice.
For a table row height, use size.row (comfortable). Don't use a compact row. Rows are read, not scanned.
When no component in the inventory fits, use plain text, a link or a heading. Don't use a new component for one article. Readers come for the words; extra parts pull the eye away from them.
For a section heading, use type.heading. Don't use bold body text. Clear headings let readers skim a long guide and find their place again.
For a text in a table cell, use type.data. Don't use a mono font. It equals body here. Tables are rare and read row by row. Cells use the reading face, so a row reads like a sentence.
Between groups, use space.gap.group. Don't use space.gap.default. A clear step between groups gives the reader a place to pause.
Inside a table cell, use space.inset.cell-x. Don't use narrow cell padding. Rows are read, not scanned. Cells get room like text does.
Item's sm size isn't used. Many readers are on phones, and rows are read, not scanned.

items.text: For the action that completes the task, use button primary, one per section. Don't use two primaries side by side. One clear action per section. Two primaries make the reader choose before they have read.
For a title of a form page, use type.title. Don't use type.display. Subscribe and account pages share the calm article title. The brand shows in the serif, not in size.
Inside a button or input, use space.inset.control-x. Don't use padding set by eye. Wide padding gives each rare action room, so a button feels as calm as the text.

For the main action on a screen, use size.control.large. Don't use a taller button for the main action. It is the same height as the default here. Actions are rare and calm. Color marks the main one; a bigger button would shout over the text.
Button's primary variant. One clear action per section.
Button's large size isn't used. Attention belongs to the text: one clear action per section, at the normal size.
Field's horizontal orientation isn't used. Forms are rare and short; stacking keeps the reading column.
Input group's block-start align isn't used. Search is one line, and forms are rare and short.
Input group's block-end align isn't used. Search is one line, and forms are rare and short.

items.text: For a hero line or key number, use type.display. Don't use type.display on article titles. On the landing hero only. One big serif line opens the publication. Articles keep calm titles, so the text gets the attention.
For a supporting text, use type.caption. Don't use type.body. Captions use the quiet interface face. Dates and notes never compete with the article.
For a edges and dividers, use border-width.default. Don't use a heavy rule. A thin edge stays quiet beside long text. The words carry the page, not the lines.
For a panel opens, use motion.duration.panels. Don't use an instant pop. A relaxed open guides the reader to the new panel without a jolt.
For the curve of any move, use motion.easing.standard. Don't use a bounce. A calm ease-out settles softly and never pulls the eye from the text.
For a hero or launch moment, use no hero motion: the landing stays still. Don't use an animated headline. Attention belongs to the text. A moving headline pulls the eye away from it.
For an icon beside text, use size.icon and icon.stroke-width. Don't use a filled or colored icon. Quiet outline icons sit beside the words and never outshine the text.

For the main action on a screen, use size.control.large. Don't use a taller button for the main action. It is the same height as the default here. Actions are rare and calm. Color marks the main one; a bigger button would shout over the text.
Button's large size isn't used. Attention belongs to the text: one clear action per section, at the normal size.
Field's horizontal orientation isn't used. Forms are rare and short; stacking keeps the reading column.
Empty's default variant isn't used. Attention belongs to the text: the invitation is in words, not a picture.
Item's muted variant isn't used. Every row in the reading list weighs the same; attention belongs to the text.

items.text: For a selected row or item, use color.surface.selected. Don't use bold text only. A tint shows the choice clearly on warm paper.
For a link, use color.text.link, underlined. Don't use color without underline. Readers expect links to be underlined inside text.
For an icon with no label, use not used: always add a word. Don't use an icon button. Occasional visitors do not know icons.
For an action on one row or item, use button ghost with a word. Don't use an icon on its own. Occasional visitors need the word.
For a parts of one item, use space.gap.tight. Don't use space.gap.default. An icon and its word sit close. Readers who visit now and then see one item, not two.
Button's ghost variant. Alternatives as a text link, and row actions with a word.
Button's icon size isn't used. Occasional visitors do not know icons: always add a word.
Button's disabled state isn't used. Keep it enabled and explain on press: visitors see the interface fresh each time.
Input group's inline-start align. The search icon before the text, with the visible label above the field.
Input group's inline-end align. The clear button after the text, with a word: occasional visitors do not know icons.

items.text: For a paragraph or help text, use type.body, at most 65 characters a line. Don't use type.caption. A large size and short lines make long text easy on the eyes.
When no component in the inventory fits, use plain text, a link or a heading. Don't use a new component for one article. Readers come for the words; extra parts pull the eye away from them.
For a items in a list or a form row, use space.gap.default. Don't use space.gap.tight. Items in a list need air, so each one reads on its own.
Between groups, use space.gap.group. Don't use space.gap.default. A clear step between groups gives the reader a place to pause.
Inside a card, panel or dialog, use space.inset.container. Don't use text that touches the card edge. Generous padding frames each card like a page in a magazine.

outcomes-q2.why: Losing your place in an article breaks the read.

items.text: For a delete or remove, use button secondary with the full verb, then confirm with Button danger. Don't use button primary. Naming the verb and confirming prevents a mistake.
For a section heading, use type.heading. Don't use bold body text. Clear headings let readers skim a long guide and find their place again.
For a control that is not available yet, use opacity.disabled. Don't use hiding the control. A faded control keeps its place. Hiding it would move the page and lose the reader's place.
Button's secondary variant. The first step of a delete, with the full verb, before the confirm.
Button's danger variant. The confirm of a delete, with the full verb. Deleting a draft is rare and final.

items.text: For an alternative or cancel, use button ghost as a text link. Don't use a second boxed button. A link feels lighter and does not compete.
Inside a button or input, use space.inset.control-x. Don't use padding set by eye. Wide padding gives each rare action room, so a button feels as calm as the text.
Inside a card, panel or dialog, use space.inset.container. Don't use text that touches the card edge. Generous padding frames each card like a page in a magazine.
For an option in a menu or list, use radius.option. Don't use radius.control. The option corner nests inside the menu corner. Soft, even curves keep the warm tone.
For a something that grows past one line, use radius.element. Don't use radius.surface. Text areas and list items share the control corner, so a form reads as one family.
For a corners of cards, menus and dialogs, use radius.surface. Don't use radius.control. Softer corners on cards and menus feel warm, like good paper.
For a panel opens, use motion.duration.panels. Don't use an instant pop. A relaxed open guides the reader to the new panel without a jolt.
For the curve of any move, use motion.easing.standard. Don't use a bounce. A calm ease-out settles softly and never pulls the eye from the text.
Button's ghost variant. Alternatives as a text link, and row actions with a word.

why: radius.8: We use an 8px corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a warm tone, by brand convention. A rounded radius does this by curving the edge enough to feel soft, while the sides stay straight. So controls feel friendly next to long text and never compete with it, because the brand is warm (brand.q1), corners are rounded (shape.values) and each screen holds one idea (content.q2).

radius.pill: We use a pill corner for badges in order to give status a role of its own, apart from the 8px controls. A full radius does this by rounding both ends into a capsule. So a status sits softly in the text and never reads as a button, because badges get their own corner (shape.roles) and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

radius.8: We use an 8px corner for menu options in order to keep nesting by the relation: the 12px surface corner minus the panel's 4px padding. The inner radius does this by following the outer curve at the padding's distance. So an option's curve runs parallel to its menu's curve, because surfaces take 12px (shape.roles, brand.q1) and the panel's padding is 4px (spacing.values).

radius.8: We use the 8px control corner for boxes that grow in order to keep their role, as objects of one family, by inheritance from the control corner. The same radius does this by giving a list item or a text area the curve of the controls beside it. So fields and rows read as one family, because the control corner is rounded, not a pill (shape.values), and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

radius.12: We use a 12px corner for article cards, menus and dialogs in order to make each card read as a separate object, in a warm tone by brand convention. A larger radius does this by breaking the outline with a curve wider than the 8px controls inside it. So a card reads as one calm object on the page, because containers get their own corner (shape.roles, shape.count) and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

brand-q3.answer: A reading serif, with a sans for the interface
brand-q3.why: Source Serif 4 for reading and headings, Inter for labels and captions: a good magazine's text with a quiet interface.

items.label: Readability
items.text: Source Serif 4 is a reading serif made for long text; its optical sizes keep body text open and even.

items.label: Legibility
items.text: Labels and captions sit in Inter, a sans with a tall x-height that stays clear at small sizes.

items.label: Scalability
items.text: Source Serif 4's optical sizes adjust the design from caption to display, so one family spans the scale.

items.label: Numerals
items.text: Data is rare here; numbers sit in the reading serif, set in running text rather than tables.

items.label: Scripts and languages
items.text: Both cover Latin, Cyrillic and Greek; Hebrew and Arabic need another face, chosen to match.

items.label: Recognition
items.text: The brand shows in type, not in color, so the serif is the brand.

items.label: Familiarity
items.text: Serif text reads like a book or an article, which long-form readers know.

items.label: Personality
items.text: Warm and considered, as the brand answer asks.

items.label: Performance
items.text: Two variable families, one file each.

items.label: Licensing
items.text: SIL Open Font License, both: free to embed in apps and on the web.

items.label: Fallback and pairing
items.text: Falls back to Georgia and system-ui, as its tokens say; Inter is the serif's interface pair.

radius.12: We use a 12px corner for article cards, menus and dialogs in order to make each card read as a separate object, in a warm tone by brand convention. A larger radius does this by breaking the outline with a curve wider than the 8px controls inside it. So a card reads as one calm object on the page, because containers get their own corner (shape.roles, shape.count) and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

items.text: For the corners of buttons and inputs, use radius.control (rounded). Don't use sharp corners. Rounded corners match the warm reading tone. Sharp corners feel technical next to long text.

why: radius.8: We use an 8px corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a warm tone, by brand convention. A rounded radius does this by curving the edge enough to feel soft, while the sides stay straight. So controls feel friendly next to long text and never compete with it, because the brand is warm (brand.q1), corners are rounded (shape.values) and each screen holds one idea (content.q2).

radius.pill: We use a pill corner for badges in order to give status a role of its own, apart from the 8px controls. A full radius does this by rounding both ends into a capsule. So a status sits softly in the text and never reads as a button, because badges get their own corner (shape.roles) and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

radius.8: We use the 8px control corner for boxes that grow in order to keep their role, as objects of one family, by inheritance from the control corner. The same radius does this by giving a list item or a text area the curve of the controls beside it. So fields and rows read as one family, because the control corner is rounded, not a pill (shape.values), and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

shape-lands.why: Corners show on buttons and article cards.

items.text: For a card on the page, use a border, no shadow. Don't use a strong shadow. Cards stay flat on the page; shadows are for floating things.

why: neutral.0, the same as content (surface.default): a menu stands out by its edge and its one shadow, not by its fill.
black.light.scrim: a see-through layer that dims the page behind a modal, so the dialog is the one thing to act on.

shadow.none: We use no shadow for cards in order to keep them at the page's height: on the scale only floating layers rise. The missing shade does this by leaving the card flat, set apart by space. So reading flows down the page without boxes that lift, because only menus and dialogs float (elevation.roles) and shadows are soft (elevation.values).

shadow.overlay: We use step 2 of the shadow scale for menus and dialogs in order to show their height as floating layers. The cast shade does this by a 12px offset and a 32px blur in a 16% warm brown. So a menu lifts off warm paper without a hard edge, because only what floats rises (elevation.roles) and shadows are soft (elevation.values).
neutral.50, the same as content (surface.default): a menu stands out by its edge and its one shadow, not by its fill, as in light.
black.dark.scrim: a see-through layer that dims the page behind a modal, so the dialog is the one thing to act on.

shadow.overlay-dark: We use the light shadow's shape for menus and dialogs in dark in order to show the same floating height by the dark-shade relation. The cast shade does this by the same 12px offset and 32px blur, at 50% black instead of 16% brown. So a menu still lifts off the dark page, though its shade reads weaker on dark than in light, because only what floats rises (elevation.roles) and dark ships for night reading (theming.values).

because.question: What should the brand feel like?

items.text: For a button label, use a warm verb a reader would say. Don't use "Submit" or "Click here". Buttons are part of the reading voice.
For the words of an error, use calm and helpful. Take the blame, offer the way forward. Don't use blaming the reader. A calm error keeps the reader's trust.
For a success message, use warm and brief, with what happens next. Don't use a bare "Done". A warm close invites the reader back.
For an empty state, use an invitation, not a dead end. Don't use "No items". An empty list is a chance to show what the product offers.
For a confirmation question, use gentle and clear about what changes. Don't use guilt or pressure. Readers come back when leaving felt respectful.
Toast's neutral tone. A calm note: You're all caught up.
Toast's success tone. Warm and brief, with what happens next.
Toast's danger tone. Calm and helpful: take the blame, offer the way forward.
Empty's icon variant. A quiet outline icon in a small tile, above a warm invitation to save an article.
